newsitem.title: FRANCE: French bond sales seen up 20 percent in 1997.
newsitem.headline: French bond sales seen up 20 percent in 1997.

text.p: France will need to sell about 20 percent more bonds next year than in 1996, mainly due to higher redemptions, but should have little problem meeting its target, analysts say.

The French Treasury, due to unveil its borrowing programme in the next two weeks, is expected to announce a target for government bond sales of between 600 billion and 630 billion francs, up from 520 billion in 1996, primary dealers contacted by Reuters estimated.
Most expected a target of 620 billion francs, which includes some issues in Ecu, in line with a French newspaper report published on October 15 which cited a finance ministry source.
The report said sales of long-dated government bonds, or OATs, would account for 320 billion francs of the total while shorter-dated bonds, or BTANs, would total 300 billion.

"It will be above 600 billion, I've pencilled in 620 billion but maybe that's being a little cautious...If it's less than 600 I would want to know how," David Brickman, European economist at Yamaichi International, said.
Some banking sources said the Treasury, which held a conference call with French primary dealers last week, was still mulling a figure of up to 630 billion francs.
Iain Lindsay, senior bond analyst at Credit Lyonnais, said he was not too concerned about the prospect of an increase in the funding target.

"Accounting for OAT sales to private individuals and Ecu auctions, the 1997 French franc supply target is likely to be 23.5 billion per auction, which is not a marked increase on the supply rate during the first quarter of 1996," he said.
The main reason for higher 1997 redemptions is the expiry of the so-called "Balladur bond", issued by the government of former prime minister Edouard Balladur, which expires in July.
"The big issue is how they fund the Balladur bond," Joanne Perez, strategist at Merrill Lynch in Paris, said. "I suspect they will look at the way the first few auctions go."
"The Balladur bond is a large redemption, but I think they will frontload and keep up a steady pace (of issuance) throughout the year," Brickman said.

The Treasury has kept up a heady pace of issuance throughout 1996, taking advantage of excess liquidity among French domestic investors and a bullish bond market environment, leaving it comfortably ahead of its 1996 funding target.

As a result it has already started buying back some of bonds due to mature 1997. It said on December 6 it had bought back 10 billion francs of bonds, trimming the amount of the Balladur bond outstanding to 94.4 billion francs.

Bond analysts said total OAT and BTAN redemptions in 1997 would be 376 billion francs. While this means the Treasury will have to raise the money to repay investors, it's likely that it will be reinvested chiefly in French bonds, they said.
France also has to raise a further 284 billion francs to fund next year's central government budget deficit -- giving a total funding requirement for next year of 660 billion francs.
Some of that funding may come either from bill issues or from extra money raised this year, analysts said.

"The deficit should pretty much fund itself," Joanne Perez at Merrill Lynch, said. Flows of money into life assurance would also continue to support the market even if these did not match 1996's bumper year, she said.

Analysts said the TEC 10 variable rate bond, which the Treasury issued for the first time in April, could prove to be a useful weapon in the Treasury's armoury and that it may also issue variable rate bonds with different maturities.

"The TEC 10 will form an ever increasing proportion of OATs to be sold," Brickman said. "As the perception grows in the second half of next year that rates have got to go up at some stage the TEC 10 will be even more vital," he said.
"If we are going to see any (bond market) correction the TEC will give an alternative investment vehicle," Perez said.

Banking sources said the Treasury had recently shelved plans to issue a five-year variable rate bond based on the TEC 10 index, but was ready to issue longer-dated variable rate bonds with maturities of 12 or 15 years if there were enough demand.
